The data reveals a pronounced inverse relationship between company size and forecast error. Mid-cap firms were forecast most accurately, with average percentage errors of 28.7% (Y1), 15.7% (Y2), and 16.1% (Y3) — a counterintuitive pattern likely reflecting the more stable, domestically-oriented business models of firms such as HUDCO and REC, which generated sub-15% errors across most metrics. Large-caps produced substantially worse aggregate results (Y1: 106.7%, Y2: 112.9%, Y3: 123.0%), though this average is heavily distorted by catastrophic outliers: ICICIBANK's Y2 revenue error reached -1,067%, and ONGC's Y1 net income error hit -1,308%, both attributable to unit-of-measurement mismatches and corporate restructuring events the model failed to anticipate. Small-caps were the least accurate segment overall (Y1: 126.1%, Y2: 147.2%), with KEC's Y1 EPS error reaching -1,884% and SKIPPER producing >90% errors on revenue and net income across all horizons — firms experiencing rapid transformations that no backward-looking training corpus can adequately model.

## 2. Accuracy Degradation by Forecast Horizon

Horizon-based degradation is unambiguous across all segments. For large-caps, average error escalated from 106.7% at Y1 to 123.0% at Y3, a deterioration of 16.3 percentage points. Mid-caps showed an unusual pattern: Y1 errors (28.7%) improved at Y2 (15.7%) before stabilising at Y3 (16.1%), suggesting the model may have front-loaded excessive conservatism in near-term estimates. Small-cap errors worsened sharply from Y1 (126.1%) to Y2 (147.2%) before retreating marginally at Y3 (121.6%), reflecting high variance rather than systematic bias. Direction accuracy — the binary correctness of growth trajectory — remained persistently weak at 43.3% for large-caps and 33.3% for both mid- and small-caps, the latter performing below random chance. These figures confirm that temporal uncertainty compounds model limitations, and three-year forecasts should be treated as directional indications only, not point estimates.

## 3. Baseline vs. Alternative Strategy Performance

The Full-Report Chain-of-Thought (CoT) strategy did not demonstrate consistent superiority over the P&L-only baseline. For well-behaved large-caps such as HDFC Bank, the alt strategy materially improved net income accuracy (Y3 error: 3.49% vs. 26.09% baseline) and revenue accuracy (Y3: 8.13% vs. 39.13%). Similarly, for INFY, the alt strategy produced a Y3 EPS error of just 1.09% versus the baseline's 7.67%. However, for ONGC and ICICIBANK, both strategies collapsed symmetrically, indicating that the underlying data confusion — not the reasoning framework — drove the failure. For TCS, the alt strategy paradoxically performed worse (Y3 revenue error: 11.94% vs. 13.36% baseline, but net income error: 18.96% vs. 11.55%). On average, the alt strategy's advantage was modest and inconsistent: it delivered meaningful gains in approximately 40% of cases, suggesting that richer context helps only when the model correctly interprets it.

## 4. Earnings Surprise Signal

The earnings surprise signal — defined as the divergence between forecasted and actual EPS relative to the prevailing stock price — showed limited predictive power for short-term returns. Direction accuracy across the 20-stock universe averaged just 38.3% for large-caps and 33.3% for mid- and small-caps, implying the signal is unreliable as a standalone trade trigger. Even where EPS directional accuracy was reasonable (INFY baseline at 0.85% Y1 error; TCS at -5.50%), the corresponding stock price forecasts diverged significantly from actuals, undermining trade signal construction. Without a formal backtested return attribution, a precise NIFTY50 outperformance rate cannot be calculated from the available data; however, given that directional accuracy in the underlying earnings signal averages below 40% — worse than a coin flip for mid- and small-caps — the signal in its current form would be expected to underperform a passive NIFTY50 strategy on a risk-adjusted basis.
